content:
A young person writes a poem about feeling empty, shows it to a parent, and is told that it is forbidden, because Muslims do not feel that way. Many have heard some form of it. The claim is wrong, and the harm it does is real: it teaches a person in pain that the pain is a sin and that silence is the pious reply.

These seven points set out what the Quran, the Prophet's sayings and the Muslim medical tradition say about grief, sadness and depression. Each is graded by how firm it is. The article concerns the claim that such feelings are un-Islamic. It does not diagnose anyone, and it is not a substitute for care. If you are in danger of harming yourself, contact your local emergency number or a crisis line now and tell a person you trust.

When Joseph was lost, his father Jacob "turned away from them and said, 'Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,' and his eyes became white from grief, for he was a suppressor of it" (12:84). Asked why he kept weeping, he answers, "I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know" (12:86).[1]

The Quran does not rebuke him. It records his grief, the loss of his sight to it, and his complaint to God, and it gives the story the weight of a whole chapter. A believer who grieves so that the eyes fail is, on the Quran's own showing, in the company of a prophet.

It helps to notice what the grief did not do. Jacob did not stop believing, and he did not stop speaking to God. He said that he complained of his grief to God alone and that he knew from God what his sons did not. Earlier in the story he says that "patience is most fitting" (12:83), and the patience contains the weeping. A reader who thinks that patience means a dry eye has not read the chapter.

Strength: firm. The verses are explicit.

In labour, Mary said, "Oh, I wish I had died before this and was in oblivion, forgotten" (19:23). Job called to his Lord, "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful" (21:83). Jonah called out "within the darknesses", "There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers" (21:87).[2]

Mary's words are a wish to be dead, spoken in distress. The Quran sets them down and goes on to give her comfort and a stream of water, and the rest of the account is mercy. Nothing in the passage treats the wish as a sin that ends the matter. Job and Jonah speak to God directly, in the words they have. Mary speaks aloud in her pain, and the Quran answers her with comfort and not with reproach.

There is a lesson in the order of the details. The Quran does not hide the wish from its audience, and it does not turn it into a moral. In Mary's case, the scene continues with a voice that calls from beneath her, "Do not grieve" (19:24), and with food and water at hand. The text meets distress with practical care. A modern reader may take from that a plain point: when someone says she wishes she were dead, the answer in the Quran is to listen and to provide, and not to scold.

Strength: firm that the words are recorded without rebuke. Reading Mary's wish as a model for ours would be going beyond the text, and the entry makes no such claim.

Anas reported that the Prophet ﷺ took his dying son Ibrāhīm, kissed him and smelled him, and that his eyes shed tears. When ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf said, "Even you are weeping?", he answered, "This is mercy," and wept more. Then he said, "The eyes shed tears and the heart is grieved, and we will not say except what pleases our Lord. O Ibrāhīm, indeed we are grieved by your separation."[3]

The answer matters twice. It says that grief is permitted and that it is a form of mercy, and it draws the boundary: no complaint against God's decree, no wailing that accuses. Within that boundary the heart may be sad and the eyes may weep.

Elsewhere in the same tradition, the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have prayed and wept for others, and the Companions are described in tears at his death. A theology that forbade sorrow would have had to forbid the best-known scenes of its founding generation. The sources do not forbid them. They teach a mourner what to say and what to avoid, and that is a different thing from teaching that a mourner should feel nothing.

Strength: firm. The report is in al-Bukhārī.

Anas also reported that the Prophet ﷺ used to say, "O Allah, I seek refuge with You from worry and grief, from incapacity and laziness, from cowardice and miserliness, from being heavily in debt and from being overpowered by men."[4]

The prayer names two states that people today call anxiety and low mood. It asks for refuge from them, as one asks for refuge from debt. A man who prays this way does not think the states are sins. He treats them as burdens that can fall on a person and from which God can protect.

The Prophet's own words also leave room for ordinary human feeling: a believer need not feel cheerful to be a believer. Strength: firm that the supplication is authentic. What it implies for ordinary sadness is an inference from the wording, though a natural one.

God says that he will test people "with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits", and tells the Prophet to give good news to the patient, who say, "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return" (2:155 to 156). He says, "with hardship will be ease", twice in two verses (94:5 to 6), and "Allah does not charge a soul except with that within its capacity" (2:286).[5]

The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that no fatigue, disease, sorrow, sadness, hurt or distress befalls a Muslim, even the prick of a thorn, but God expiates some of his sins for it.[6] The report treats sadness as something that befalls a believer and carries meaning, and it does not treat it as a sign that the believer has failed.

Strength: moderate. The verses are firm. The promise of "ease" is a promise about the end, and the verses do not say that pain disappears when one prays. A person who is still in pain has not been contradicted by them.

A group of Bedouin asked the Prophet ﷺ whether they should make use of medical treatment. He said, "Make use of medical treatment, for Allah has not made a disease without appointing a remedy for it, with the exception of one disease, namely old age."[7] Al-Bukhārī has the same teaching in the form that there is no disease that God has created except that he has also created its treatment.[8]

In the ninth century Abū Zayd al-Balkhī wrote a book on the health of bodies and souls, which treats depression and anxiety among other conditions and distinguishes kinds of low mood by their cause. Recent studies describe him as separating a sadness that has an outward cause from one that arises within, and recommending different care for each.[9] Popular accounts claim more than that, for example that he invented talk therapy, and those claims should be treated with caution.

Strength: firm on the command to seek treatment. Moderate on al-Balkhī, whose work I read about in modern studies and not in the original.

No verse or report forbids writing a poem about emptiness. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that some poetry contains wisdom.[10] The idea that a Muslim does not feel empty or low has no basis in the Quran or in the Prophet's sayings, where grief, tears and appeals to God fill many pages.

The sources also do not say that prayer alone is the answer to every condition. They ask for patience, prayer and trust, and they ask for treatment, and a person with a serious and lasting low mood should see a doctor and a counsellor, as she would for a lasting pain. Some Muslim communities have treated mental illness as shame. That is a failure of the community, and it has no support in the texts above.

Strength: firm on what the sources do not say. This article cannot say what is happening in any person's life. If it is a danger to you, please speak to someone today.

The bottom line

The claim that Muslims do not feel sad or empty fails against the sources. Five points are firm: a prophet's grief is in the Quran, Mary, Job and Jonah spoke their distress and were not rebuked, the Prophet ﷺ wept at his son's death and called it mercy, he asked God for refuge from worry and grief, and the command to seek treatment is in the sayings. One is moderate: the promise of ease, and the account of al-Balkhī, which I read second-hand.

The Muslim tradition does not ask a person to hide pain. It gives her words for it, permission for it, a duty to seek a cure for it, and a boundary around it: no complaint against God's decree. That is the only thing it forbids. Allāhu aʿlam.

Notes

  1. Quran 12:83, 12:84 and 12:86, Saheeh International translation, read on the Quran.com API.
  2. Quran 19:23 to 19:25, 21:83 and 21:87, Saheeh International.
  3. Sahih al-Bukhari 1303, report of Anas ibn Mālik (read in the English text of the hadith-api edition; the printed page was not checked).
  4. Sahih al-Bukhari 6369, report of Anas ibn Mālik (same source).
  5. Quran 2:155 to 156, 94:5 to 6 and 2:286, Saheeh International.
  6. Sahih al-Bukhari 5641, report of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī and Abū Hurayra (same source).
  7. Sunan Abi Dawud 3855, report of Usāma ibn Sharīk, graded sahih by al-Albānī and others in the same edition.
  8. Sahih al-Bukhari 5678, report of Abū Hurayra (same source).
  9. Abū Zayd al-Balkhī, Maṣāliḥ al-abdān wa-l-anfus ("The sustenance of bodies and souls"), the chapter on relieving depression; his classification is as summarised in a 2023 article in the journal Psikis and other modern studies read on the web. The original was not read, and the claim that he invented talk therapy is not repeated here.
  10. Sahih al-Bukhari 6145, report of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, "some poetry contains wisdom" (same source).
